Maintenance plans as a growth engine

Maintenance plans are often sold as a discount. Run well, they are the most reliable growth channel an HVAC business has.

Savvy Team Growth strategy · Savvy Post Marketing

Published September 2, 2026 · 5 min read

More than a membership card

Many HVAC companies sell maintenance plans, but few treat them as a marketing channel. The plan becomes a line on an invoice, renewal rates drift, and visits get squeezed into whatever time is left. Treated deliberately, a plan does three jobs at once: it smooths demand, it keeps customers loyal and it surfaces replacement opportunities early.

Job one: smooth the calendar

Two visits a year is a lot of scheduled work. If those visits are booked into the quietest weeks, the plan becomes a tool for keeping technicians busy when the phone is slow. Booking them into the busiest weeks does the opposite.

  • Offer plan members priority booking in exchange for flexible visit windows.
  • Book spring tune-ups in the weeks before cooling demand starts.
  • Book fall visits before the first cold snap, not after it.

Job two: keep customers for years

A customer on a plan has a reason to call you first. They also hear from you twice a year, which means your name is the one they remember when something breaks. Retention rarely shows up in a campaign report, but it is the foundation of every other channel.

“The best time to win a replacement is during a maintenance visit, not after a breakdown.”

Job three: find replacement work early

Each visit is a chance to document the condition of the equipment: age, efficiency, recurring issues. When a system is approaching the end of its life, the customer hears about it calmly, with options and time to plan, rather than in an emergency.

In practice · HVAC

A simple “system health” rating left after every visit, with ageing systems flagged for a planned-replacement conversation in the next shoulder season.

Make renewals a campaign

Renewal is the moment most plans leak members. Instead of sending an invoice, remind customers what the plan did for them this year: visits completed, issues caught, priority calls answered. Then make renewing a single click or call.

Example renewal sequence
TimingMessage
30 days beforeYour year with us: what we checked and found
14 days beforeRenew in one click, keep your priority booking
On the dateFriendly reminder from the technician who visits you
7 days afterLast call, with an easy way to ask questions

Train technicians to have the conversation

Technicians are the face of the plan. They see the equipment, they know its condition and customers trust them more than any ad. But many are uncomfortable “selling”. Reframe it: the job is to explain what they found and what the options are, not to close a deal.

A short checklist helps. Show the customer anything that needs attention, explain what happens if it is left, and give a clear next step: monitor it, repair it, or plan a replacement. Then record it in the CRM so the office can follow up at the right time, ideally in a quieter week.

Finally, measure the plan like a channel. Track members, renewal rate, visits completed on schedule and the value of work that started from a maintenance visit. Those four numbers tell you whether the plan is growing the business or just discounting it.

Where to start

  1. Count active plan members and last year’s renewal rate.
  2. Move next season’s visits into your slowest weeks.
  3. Add a documented condition rating to every visit.

Key takeaways

  • A maintenance plan is a retention system, not a discount.
  • Schedule visits into shoulder seasons on purpose.
  • Every visit should end with a documented system condition.
  • Renewals deserve a campaign, not an invoice.
